title: Wireless without the guesswork
summary: Make sense of bands, channels, and interference.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: Wireless clients share radio airtime. A strong signal does not guarantee a fast connection when neighboring devices compete on the same channel. The 2.4 GHz band generally reaches farther through obstacles than higher bands but is often crowded. The 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands offer additional channel space for compatible equipment. Available channels and power limits depend on the local regulatory region, so configure devices for their actual location.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: A channel occupies a slice of radio spectrum, and wider channels combine more spectrum to increase potential throughput. In a dense office, that wider footprint can overlap more neighbors and reduce effective performance. Use a wireless analyzer to inspect nearby activity, then compare measured performance before and after a change. Client support matters too: an older radio cannot gain a new band through an access-point setting alone. Bluetooth and NFC serve different short-range tasks rather than replacing a wireless LAN.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
